chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Khalid from Abu al-Bakhtari Wahb ibn Wahb from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father from Ali (peace be upon him) that he said:

"If it is the end of the surah, it suffices for you to bow with it." This does not contradict the report of al-Halabi mentioned earlier, because we interpret this report as referring to one who prays with a group who cannot prostrate, stand, and recite al-Hamd; for there is no harm in him bowing with them. And the report of al-Habi and others who narrated this is interpreted as referring to one who is able to do so by being alone. What indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.أَجْزَأَكَ: It suffices for you / It is acceptable for you.
key_terms.اَلسَّجْدَةَ: The final surah (chapter) of the Quran, specifically referring to Surah As-Sajdah or any surah ending with a prostration verse in this context.
key_terms.اَلْحَمْدَ: Al-Hamd (referring to Surah Al-Fatihah or the praise recited in prayer).
key_terms.خَبَرَ اَلْحَلَبِيِّ: The report/narration of al-Halawi (a specific narrator).
key_terms.مَحْمُولٌ: Interpreted / Ascribed to a specific context.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on bowing in the final surah if one cannot prostrate?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the apparent contradiction between reports by distinguishing between the congregant (muqtadi) who prays in unison with the imam and cannot independently complete the full sequence, and the individual (mufrid) who must perform the complete ritual. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of facilitating prayer in congregational settings while maintaining strict adherence to the full form of worship for those who are able. The text emphasizes that the permissibility of bowing without a separate prostration is context-dependent, reflecting the practical realities of communal prayer dynamics.
